blocks.text: “Don't say yes,” Miss Smallweed answers, “because I know what you girls are like. Do it without saying it. Then I may begin to believe you.”

Charley swallows a big mouthful of tea to show that she accepts this. In doing so she scatters the Druid-like ruins of bread and butter so fast that Miss Smallweed tells her not to eat greedily. Greedy eating, she remarks, is disgusting “in you girls.” Charley might have found it harder to answer Miss Smallweed's views on the general subject of girls. But then there is a knock at the door.
“See who it is, and don't chew when you open it!” cries Judy.

Charley goes away to open the door. Miss Smallweed uses this chance to push the rest of the bread and butter together into a heap. She also throws two or three dirty tea-cups into the basin of tea, where the tea is going down like the sea at low tide. This is a hint that she thinks the eating and drinking are finished.
“Now! Who is it, and what's wanted?” says Judy in her sharp, bad-tempered way.
It seems to be someone called “Mr. George.” Mr. George walks straight in. Nobody announces him, and there is no ceremony.
“Whew!” says Mr. George. “It's hot in here. Always a fire, eh? Well! Perhaps you are right to get used to one.” Mr. George says this last remark to himself, as he nods to Grandfather Smallweed.
“Ho! It's you!” cries the old gentleman. “How de do? How de do?”
“So-so,” replies Mr. George, taking a chair. “I have had the honour of seeing your granddaughter before. My respects to you, miss.”
“This is my grandson,” says Grandfather Smallweed. “You ha'n't seen him before. He is in the law, and not much at home.”

“My respects to him, too! He is like his sister. He is very like his sister. He is devilish like his sister,” says Mr. George. He puts great stress on that last word, and the stress is not entirely a compliment.
“And how is the world treating you, Mr. George?” Grandfather Smallweed asks, slowly rubbing his legs.
“Pretty much as usual. Like a football.”

He is a dark, sunburnt man of fifty. He is well built and good-looking, with short curly dark hair, bright eyes and a broad chest. His strong, muscular hands are as sunburnt as his face. They have clearly been used to a fairly rough life. One curious thing about him is the way he sits forward on his chair. He seems, from long habit, to be leaving space for some uniform or equipment that he has now completely given up. His step, too, is steady and heavy. It would go well with a heavy clash and jingle of spurs. He is clean-shaved now. But his mouth is set as if his upper lip had known a great moustache for years. He sometimes lays the open palm of his broad brown hand on that lip, and this suggests the same thing. All in all, one might guess that Mr. George was once a trooper, a soldier on horseback.

Mr. George is a very special contrast to the Smallweed family. No trooper was ever lodged in a household more unlike him. It is like a broad heavy sword next to a little oyster-knife. His full-grown body stands against their small, stunted forms. His large manner, which fills any amount of room, stands against their little, narrow, pinched ways. His loud ringing voice stands against their sharp, thin tones. They are opposites in the strongest and the strangest way. He sits in the middle of the grim parlour, leaning a little forward, with his hands on his thighs and his elbows out square. He looks as if he would swallow up the whole family if he stayed there long. He would swallow up the whole four-roomed house too, the extra little back-kitchen and all.
“Do you rub your legs to rub life into 'em?” he asks Grandfather Smallweed, after looking round the room.
“Why, it's partly a habit, Mr. George, and—yes—it partly helps the circulation, the flow of my blood,” he replies.
